science.title: Age and the association between admission platelet count and in-hospital mortality in critically ill children
science.description: To investigate whether the prognostic weight of admission coagulation markers for in-hospital mortality varies with age in critically ill children. We retrospectively analyzed children admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) in the Pediatric Intensive Care database, with in-hospital mortality as the primary outcome. Inclusion required at least one valid coagulation measurement from 6 h before to 24 h after ICU admission. Logistic regression examined interactions between age and six coagulation markers—platelet count, prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), international normalized ratio (INR), fibrinogen, and D-dimer—adjusting for sex, ICU, admission lactate, vasoactive prescriptions, and diagnostic category. Sensitivity analyses assessed nonlinear relationships, age grouping, additional laboratory adjustment, exclusions, missing data, and selection bias. A total of 11,508 children were included, with 693 in-hospital deaths (6.0%). The primary platelet model included 11,330 children and 657 deaths. Only platelet count met the Bonferroni threshold for an adjusted age interaction (odds ratio [OR] 0.957, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.928–0.986 per 1-SD higher platelet count per additional year; P = 0.004). With a nonlinear platelet main effect and a linear platelet×age interaction, the interaction attenuated to OR 0.969 (95% CI 0.942–0.997; nominal P = 0.032). The unadjusted INR interaction was significant (OR 0.977, 95% CI 0.964–0.990; P < 0.001), but the adjusted interaction was not (OR 0.999, 95% CI 0.987–1.011; P = 0.877). Age-stratified platelet associations were generally stronger in older groups but were not monotonic. Overall interaction tests were not significant with spline models for platelet count, age, or both (P = 0.174, 0.065, and 0.629), or with three broad age groups (P = 0.088). Evidence for age-related variation in the platelet–mortality association was sensitive to model specification. The finding remains exploratory and requires external validation before considering age-specific platelet weighting in clinical scores.

science.title: Methyl jasmonate (MeJA) as an elicitor enhances tomato resistance through ROS and digestive enzyme inhibition against Helicoverpa armigera (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae)
science.description: Methyl jasmonate (MeJA) is a central regulator of plant defense, yet the physiological consequences of MeJA-induced defenses for herbivorous insects remain incompletely resolved across multiple levels of herbivore performance. Here, we investigated how exogenous MeJA treatment of tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) modulates plant oxidative defenses and the subsequent digestive, antioxidant, and nutritional physiology of Helicoverpa armigera larvae. MeJA elicitation induced a significant, dose-dependent H₂O₂-associated response in tomato leaves, with DAB-derived staining extending across approximately 98% of the leaf area at 1 mM MeJA, accompanied by a 45% increase in peroxidase (POD) activity. Feeding third-instar larvae on MeJA-elicited foliage increased mortality from 13% in controls to > 60% at 1 mM MeJA and reduced larval length by up to 68%. These effects coincided with pronounced alterations in midgut digestive physiology, with trypsin, chymotrypsin, α-amylase, and lipase activities decreasing by approximately 45–65%. Larval antioxidant responses were likewise markedly altered, with catalase (CAT) activity declining by approximately 99.7% and POD activity by approximately 42–47.9%, consistent with a substantially reduced enzymatic antioxidant response. These physiological changes were accompanied by marked alterations in whole-organism performance, with relative growth rate (RGR) declining from 1.56 to 0.00017 mg/g/day, corresponding to an approximately 99.99% reduction, while efficiency of conversion of ingested food (ECI) decreased from 3.09 to 0.28% (approximately 91% reduction). Although approximate digestibility (AD) increased at higher MeJA concentrations, this increase was not accompanied by improved growth or food-conversion efficiency, indicating that greater apparent digestibility did not translate into more effective nutrient utilization. Collectively, these findings show that MeJA-induced tomato defenses are associated with coordinated alterations in the digestive, antioxidant, and nutritional physiology of H. armigera, coinciding with impaired larval growth and survival. By integrating plant oxidative responses with multiple physiological dimensions of herbivore performance, this study provides a broader physiological perspective on MeJA-elicited tomato resistance and highlights interconnected physiological responses that warrant further mechanistic and ecological investigation.
